explanation: Fires on cognition verbs, mainly ' know'/' knew'/' understand' (and sometimes ' thought'), when they directly follow a subject pronoun or name, as in 'I know', 'I don't understand', 'you know'. It also fires on the punctuation that opens a thought or quote ('I thought:', 'thought to myself,'). Speech verbs like ' said' get weaker activation, and unrelated tokens get little.

Fires on a wide, varied set of tokens: ' you' in cookie-consent boilerplate ('By using this website you'), ' include' after 'traits', commas and periods that close a clause, code tokens, and digits in phone numbers or ISSNs. I can see no shared lexical or semantic trigger.

Fires on a word-stem subword piece inside a longer word that is split into several tokens. Strongest on Russian verb stems (смотр, вид, сохран, объясн); it also fires on English and Latin-like stems such as 'infer', 'iod', 'fer', 'refer', 'interfer', 'ver'. It responds mostly to the token being a mid-word root, not to the context.

Fires on tokens about spatial dimensions and 3D geometry. Strongest on the second ' x' in 'L x W x H' size specs and on the third value in dimension lists; also on '3D'/'3d', 'depth', 'non-planar', 'cylinder', 'vertical', and the third coordinate in vectors or R^3. Ordinary text gives little.

Fires on structural tokens that open the next element of a list or an argument list. Examples are '(' after 'function' in JS or after 'aims are:' before '(1)', a second parameter like ' action', list numbers like '2', and sequence words such as 'Lastly' or 'In addition'. Several top hits ('come and go', 'fists', 'weekday') do not fit this pattern.

Fires on the later part of a word or compound, usually the completing suffix or second element: 'quadr-ature', 'cardiorespir-atory', 'extramar-ital', 'rocket-prop-elled', 'goal-sc-oring', 'multi-family', 'six-day'. Some unrelated content words also fire ('finer', 'fever', 'right', 'seem'). Function words give only weak responses.

Mainly fires on approximation words before a quantity: ' about', ' roughly', ' approximately', ' nearly' (for example 'at a cost of roughly £20 million'). A separate code habit fires on '0' in 'for (i = 0;' and on type names in struct literals. The rest is miscellaneous.

Fires on many unrelated things: German word-initial pieces ('er' in 'erwartete', 'h' in 'harte', 'vor'), ' you' or ' we' in 'what you need' / 'the only thing we want', CJK bytes and characters, digits, and code tokens. I find no consistent trigger.

Fires on a mix of tokens: 'opensource' in license URLs (http://opensource.org/licenses), identifier pieces in code (Product, didFinish, aDecoder, /stretchr), sentence-initial connectives like '而' or 'Mais', CJK bytes, and word pieces in biomedical terms. It looks like a set of separate contexts rather than one concept.

Fires on the first one or two letters of a word that the tokenizer splits off as a separate piece, especially in non-English Latin-script text (French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian) and in rare technical terms. Examples: 'S'+'ouligné', ' m'+'airie', ' p'+'ustules', ' ép'+'iciers', 'Dros'+'oph'+'ila'. The token itself, a word-initial fragment of a fragmented word, is what matters.

Fires on a mix of tokens: the leading digit of a numeric answer after '-', CJK byte pieces, ' (' before unit conversions ('60 kilometres (37 miles)'), digits in years and dates, and assorted words (' whose', ' with', ' the', ' named'). I see no single pattern.

Fires on the first letter or letters of a word piece that follows a hyphen, an open parenthesis, or a split, especially 'v' and 'm' starts: '(v'ocals', 'non-sm'oking', 'age-m'atched', 'N-m'ethyl', 'shape-m'aintenance', '[[V]]illages'. Word-initial fragments after hyphens are the core trigger.

Fires on function words and word pieces in German and Scandinavian (Danish/Norwegian) text: ' zu', ' für', ' auf', ' von', ' til', ' på', ' er', ' et', and 'gesch'. It also fires weakly on German-looking pieces inside English text. English text in general gives near-zero activation.
Fires almost only on a '0' digit inside a long run of zeros (for example '000000000 +080', as in hex or timestamp strings). Everything else, including opening quotes and other tokens, stays near 1%.
